overview.text: The associative property, also called associativity, describes how a binary operation handles grouping: for three inputs a, b, and c, (a ★ b) ★ c = a ★ (b ★ c). The inputs stay in the same order; only the parentheses move, so this differs from commutativity, which changes their order. For real-number addition and multiplication, regrouping leaves the sum or product unchanged—for example, (7 + 8) + 2 = 7 + (8 + 2). This can make calculations easier by letting you combine convenient pairs first. Subtraction and division are not associative, so regrouping them can change the answer. Associativity also matters beyond arithmetic: it is one of the requirements for a group in abstract algebra.

key_facts.text: In the general rule, ★ stands for an operation, and the same three inputs remain in the same order as the parentheses shift.
Real-number addition and multiplication are associative: (a + b) + c = a + (b + c), and (a · b) · c = a · (b · c).
Associativity is about grouping; commutativity is about changing the order of the inputs.
Subtraction and division are not associative: (10 − 3) − 2 = 5, while 10 − (3 − 2) = 9.
In abstract algebra, associativity is one of the defining requirements for a group, alongside an identity element and inverses.
